newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Anti-Kabila protests flare in Congo.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Kabila protests flare in Congo.

text.p: Some one-thousand students from Kinshasa University took to the streets of the capital on Saturday to protest against the self-proclaimed president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Laurent Kabila.
Witnesses said troops fired two shots in the air, scattering most of the protesters, but about 200 continued the march from the working-class Matonge district towards the city centre.
The march was much larger than an anti-Kabila demonstration on Friday.

"We want the Rwandans to leave, Kabila has sold the country," said medical student Henri Olenga. Other students said Kabila must appoint veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi to his government.
Western intelligence sources say Kabila's seven-month rebellion, triggered by ethnic Tutsis demanding citizenship, has received military assistance from Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army.

There were also street protests in the southern mining region of the former Zaire, with demonstrators denouncing the new government marching in the streets of the diamond mining centre of Mbuji-Mayi on Friday, residents said on Saturday.
They said by telephone the protest was triggered by the exclusion from the government of veteran politician Tshisekedi, who comes from Kasai and has a huge following there.
"There were lots of people demonstrating and troops fired into the air to disperse them," said one resident. The exact number of demonstrators was unclear.
Mbuji-Mayi was calm on Saturday with businesses open.
On May 17 Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) entered the capital Kinshasa, a day after long-serving president Mobutu Sese Seko fled.
In naming a new government Kabila abolished the post of prime minister, which Tshisekedi claims for himself on the basis of a 1992 national conference, although he was sacked by Mobutu.
Pro-opposition newspapers expressed alarm at the defiant stand of the new rulers after Tshisekedi's fanatical supporters took to the streets of the capital on Friday.
Kabila's government said on Friday that because his AFDL won the rebel war it had the right to decide the future.
The Potentiel newspaper said the people of the new Congo were dismayed and fearful of a return to dictatorship.
"They see from the first political acts of the new rulers that we are heading towards a single party state," it said.
"National opinion protests, and the legitimacy of the new president of the republic is already in question. Confidence is lost," it said.

After seven months of bush war to oust the cancer-stricken Mobutu, foreign minister Bizima Karaha called on him to return home with the money he stashed abroad during his 32 year rule, which the word "kleptocracy" was coined to describe.

"We are not ready to take nonsense from anyone for whatever reason, just to make sure people are happy. Liberty yes, but revolution first," Karaha told a news conference after Tshisekedi and his supporters denounced the Alliance on Friday.
Kabila's troops also fired in the air on Friday to halt a march on parliament by several hundred Tshisekedi supporters.
Tshisekedi was the most stubborn political opponent of Mobutu and has a fanatical following in Kasai and Kinshasa.
Mobutu, weakened by cancer, arrived in Morocco on Friday from Togo but an official in Rabat said on Saturday he was expected to go on to France early next month.

"President Mobutu, who was welcomed by Morocco for humanitarian reasons, is expected to leave for France as his final destination at the beginning of June unless there are complications in his health," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said Paris would consider a request for asylum but had not received one.
